lesson_title: The Shop That Never Empties: Chemical Equilibrium
hook_text: 40 people walk in every minute. 40 walk out. The crowd never changes — and that's half of matric chemistry.
clip_script: Saturday morning, busy shop. Every minute, forty people walk in and forty walk out. Count the crowd: two hundred. Count again in ten minutes: still two hundred. Has the shop gone quiet? Not even close — the doorway is churning. Constant crowd, non-stop traffic. That is chemical equilibrium: the forward reaction is the door in, the reverse reaction is the door out, and when the two rates match, the concentrations freeze while the molecules keep reacting both ways. Anyone who says the reaction stopped is counting heads through the window. Now push the system — chemistry pushes back. Dump in extra reactant and the reaction leans away, consuming it. Squeeze the gases and everything shifts toward the side with fewer molecules — less crowding. Heat an exothermic reaction? Heat is a product, so adding heat leans the system backwards, and your yield drops. That's Le Chatelier's principle: every push gets partly, never fully, undone. It's how ammonia plants trick equilibrium into feeding the world — keep stealing the product, and the frustrated reaction keeps making more. One shop, one see-saw, one principle — and a full exam question, every single year.
visual_style: A shopfront with tally counters over two doors ticking in perfect sync while the crowd number holds; then a giant hand pushing one pan of a balance and the balance leaning back, settling part-way; pipes syphoning product out of a factory vessel.
mood: Everyday bustle turned into elegant push-and-pushback logic.
pacing: Calm crowd-counting open, snappy push-back montage of the three disturbances, industrial payoff close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and own the equilibrium question that appears every single year.
